To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
maternal gestational diet can independently impact the risk of offspring metabolic disease.
Maternal obesity and maternal diet independently alter lipid processing in the placenta, and that these changes may contribute to the risk of offspring metabolic disease.
maternal diet and body composition are independent but synergistic factors in determining the risk for later life obesity-associated metabolic disease in offspring.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of maternal obesity on placental lipid processing functions and how maternal diet can be manipulated to improve placental function.

understanding how gestational obesity, independent from maternal diet, impacts placental lipid processing and how maternal diet can be used as an intervention to reduce offspring risk for later-life obesity-related disease.
understanding the mechanisms by which maternal diet impacts the placental lipid processing environment and how this impacts fetal development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

maternal diet is an important mediator of the impact of maternal obesity upon offspring metabolic health, and thus dietary interventions in obese pregnancies should be explored as a potential strategy to reduce the impact of maternal body composition upon offspring metabolic disease risk.
maternal obesity and maternal diet are two independent but interacting factors that can influence placental function and thus the health of the developing offspring.
maternal obesity and poor maternal dietary intake are both important mediators of placental lipid processing and offspring metabolic disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a maternal high fat diet in the presence of maternal obesity promotes an in utero environment that is permissive to the development of later-life metabolic disease.
maternal diet, independent of maternal body composition, is an important modulator of placental lipid handling and offspring metabolic disease risk.

a poor maternal diet is associated with the development and progression of metabolic disease in offspring, and that maternal obesity further exacerbates this risk through changes in placental lipid metabolism.
The main takeaway from our work is that

maternal diet is an underappreciated modulator of placental lipid handling processes in obesity and that altering maternal diet may be an important therapeutic strategy to improve the risk of offspring metabolic disease in obesity.
the obese maternal diet is a key mediator of offspring risk, and that maternal diet can be used to modulate placental function and thus offspring risk.
maternal diet can independently influence placental function and that this can be a mechanism for programming of offspring metabolic health.
